after: ## Land use zones and the reasons for their location
alt: A graph of land value falling steeply from the city centre, where routes meet and accessibility is highest, then more gently outwards. Bands below show the zones in order: CBD, inner city, suburbs, rural–urban fringe. High-profit users such as shops, offices and banks pay most and build upwards in the centre; users needing lots of space locate further out.
caption: Accessibility and land value sort land uses from the centre outwards.

after: ### Cities at different levels of development
alt: Two schematic city models. High-income city: a central CBD ringed by inner city, suburbs and rural–urban fringe, with old industry by the river and railway and a modern estate on the edge; the wealthiest often live furthest out. Lower-income city: a CBD with high-income housing in a sector near it and along a main road, industry along main roads, and squatter settlements around the edge on land nobody else wants.
caption: In many lower-income cities the poorest live on the edge, not the wealthiest.

after: ## Changes in land use and urban sprawl
alt: Four panels. Deindustrialisation and redevelopment: old factories and docks become offices, flats and leisure, as at London Docklands and Canary Wharf. Gentrification: wealthier people renovate older inner-city housing and prices rise. Decentralisation: shops and offices move to retail and business parks on the fringe. Urban sprawl: the built-up area spreads onto greenfield land.
caption: Cities reuse their centres and spread at their edges.

after: ## Changes in land use and urban sprawl
alt: A schematic plan of a city spreading outwards into a surrounding green belt, with a commuter village and a planned new town beyond. Effects of sprawl: loss of farmland and habitats and faster runoff; longer journeys and car dependence; commuter villages with rising house prices and closing services; and the cost of extending utilities. Responses: green belts, brownfield first, higher-density housing and new towns such as Navi Mumbai.
caption: Sprawl eats greenfield land; planners push growth onto brownfield sites and new towns.

alt: A schematic sketch map of a city with a central core, a river and railway crossing near the centre, and a ring road around the edge. Industrial area A sits by the river and railway near the centre because goods once moved by water and rail and workers walked to work. Industrial estate B sits on the ring road at the edge for lorry access and cheap, large plots with room to expand.
caption: Tie every reason to something you can see on the map.

after: ## Worked example 2: planning a case-study answer
alt: Three columns. Causes: a large commuting workforce, an old street pattern, and deliveries, taxis and buses competing for space. Attempts: the Congestion Charge from 2003, the Underground, bus and rail network, the Docklands Light Railway and cycle lanes. Evaluation: less traffic in the zone, but criticism over effects on small businesses and lower-income drivers, and public transport is costly and slow to build.
caption: Cause, attempted solution, then how well it works.
